title: Functions and headers
objectives: Write functions and declare them in a header file.

screens.title: Used before it is known
screens.prose: In Python a function can sit below the code that calls it. It only has to exist when the call runs. Here is the same layout in C++.

screens.title: Declaration or definition
screens.prose: A **declaration** gives a function's name and types and ends with `;`. A **definition** adds the body in braces, and it declares the name too.
screens.question: Tap every line that only declares a function, with no body.

Line 3 has a body in `{ }`.
Lines 1 and 2 end in `;` with no body; line 4 is a variable.

feedback.correct: Lines 1 and 2: types and a semicolon, no body.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A declaration only has no braces.

byKey.def: Line 3 has a body in braces, so it is a definition. It declares `half` too, but it is not only a declaration.
byKey.l4: `double rate = 0.04;` is a variable with a value, not a function.

explain.text: Lines 1 and 2 promise functions without bodies. Line 3 is a definition, and line 4 a variable. Parameter names in a declaration are optional, but they make it readable.

screens.title: Three files
screens.prose: Real projects split the work. `returns.h`, a **header**, holds declarations; `returns.cpp` holds the definitions. Each `.cpp` file is compiled on its own into its own object file, then the linker joins them.

lines: double annualise(double daily_vol, int days) { return daily_vol * std::sqrt(days); }
params.title: Three files and the build

screens.question: `main.cpp` calls `annualise(0.01)`. Tap the line whose body runs.

hints.text: Which file holds bodies?
Look under `// returns.cpp`.
Line 11 is the only `annualise` with braces.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the `annualise` that has a body.

byKey.l5: Line 5 only declares `annualise`; it has no body. It tells `main.cpp` the call is legal, and the linker finds the body in `returns.o`.
byKey.l16: That is the call itself. Its body is elsewhere.
byKey.l15: `#include "returns.h"` pastes in the declarations, not the bodies.

explain.text: `#include "returns.h"` pastes the header's text into `main.cpp`, so the compiler sees the declaration and accepts the call. The body on line 11 is compiled separately into `returns.o`. The linker connects the call to it.

screens.title: A default argument
screens.prose: Line 5 says `int days = 252`: a **default argument**. A call that leaves `days` out gets 252, which is why `annualise(0.01)` printed 0.158745, which is $0.01\sqrt{252}$.

lines: double annualise(double daily_vol, int days) { return daily_vol * std::sqrt(days); }
params.title: Three files and the build

screens.question: What does `annualise(0.01, 365)` return, to 4 decimal places?

hints.text: The second argument replaces the default.
Line 11 computes `daily_vol * std::sqrt(days)`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use `days = 365` in line 11.

byKey.default: That is the default, 252. Passing 365 replaces it.
byKey.sum: You multiplied by 365. Annualising multiplies by the square root of the days.

explain.text: A default fills in only when the call leaves that argument out. Here `days` is 365, so the result is $0.01 \times \sqrt{365} \approx 0.1910$. Daily volatility of 1% over a 365-day calendar annualises to about 19.1%.

screens.title: Defining a declared function
screens.prose: The header line is hidden above your code, as `#include "returns.h"` would paste it. Write the definition. `out.push_back(r)` appends to a vector, like Python's `append`. One close, or none, gives no returns.
screens.question: Define `simple_returns(prices)`: each day's return after the first, `(today - yesterday) / yesterday`.

The signature must match the declaration on line 4 exactly.
`out.push_back((prices[i] - prices[i - 1]) / prices[i - 1]);` for `i` from 1 while `i < prices.size()`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: One close has no day before it, so the list must be empty. If the program stopped, your loop read `prices[i - 1]` with `i` at 0.
byKey.test-1: From 110 to 99 is (99 − 110) / 110 = −0.1. Divide by yesterday's close, not today's.
byKey.compile: If the error mentions a declaration, make your first line match `returns.h` exactly, including `const` and `&`.

explain.text: Starting at index 1 gives each return a yesterday, so one close or none gives an empty list. Your definition matches the hidden declaration, so the two name one function.

screens.title: Where the default lives
screens.prose: The hidden header declares `double annualise(double daily_vol, int days = 252);`. A default argument is written once, in the declaration. Repeating `= 252` in the definition is an error: `redefinition of default argument`.
screens.question: Define `annualise`: the daily volatility times the square root of `days`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests, some leaving days out. Each answer is accepted within a relative 1e-9 (a zero must be exactly 0).

hints.text: `std::sqrt` from `<cmath>` takes a square root.
The default is already in the header on line 5.
`return daily_vol * std::sqrt(days);` and no `= 252` in your line.

feedback.correct: The header holds the default; the definition holds the body.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test or the compiler message.

byKey.compile: If the message says `redefinition of default argument`, delete `= 252` from your definition: the default lives in the header only.
byKey.test-1: `annualise(0.01)` should be 0.01 × √252 ≈ 0.1587. Multiply by the square root of `days`.

explain.text: Callers see only the header, so the default must be there for `annualise(0.01)` to compile in their files. The definition takes `days` as a plain parameter. Annualising a daily volatility by $\sqrt{252}$ assumes 252 trading days a year.

screens.question: The header has `#pragma once`. Why does the build still fail?

options.text: Each `.cpp` file gets its own copy of the body, so the linker finds two

options.why: g++ honours it. It stops one `.cpp` file including the header twice, which is not what happened.

options.text: The compiler should have caught it, so it is a compiler bug
options.why: Each file was compiled alone and looked fine. Only the linker sees both object files.

options.text: `simple_return` clashes with a standard library name
options.why: The message names `main.cpp` and `pricer.cpp` as the two definitions, both yours.

hints.text: `#pragma once` works within one `.cpp` file.
Line 3 names two object files, one from each `.cpp`.
Each `.cpp` pasted the header, body and all, so each object file defines `simple_return`.

feedback.correct: One body per program: in a `.cpp`, not a header.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Who sees both object files?

byKey.ignored: You expected `#pragma once` to cover the whole program. It covers one `.cpp` at a time, and each of the two pasted its own copy of the body.

explain.text: `#include` pastes the header into each `.cpp`, so `main.o` and `pricer.o` both contain the body. `#pragma once` only stops a repeat within one file. Put the declaration in the header and the body in one `.cpp`, or mark it `inline`.

screens.question: A teammate adds `int days = 252` to the definition in `returns.cpp` only, and removes it from the header. What happens to `annualise(0.01)` in `main.cpp`?

options.text: It no longer compiles: `main.cpp` sees no default

options.why: `main.cpp` is compiled from the header alone. It never sees `returns.cpp`, so it never sees the default.
C++ never invents a value for a missing argument. Without a visible default, the call is an error.

options.text: It compiles, but the linker fails
options.why: The problem appears earlier: the compiler rejects a call with too few arguments.

hints.text: When `main.cpp` is compiled, which files does the compiler read?

feedback.correct: Callers see the header, so defaults go there.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each `.cpp` is compiled on its own.

explain.text: `main.cpp` is compiled with only the header's text, so it sees a function that needs two arguments. The call with one is a compile error. Defaults belong in the declaration that callers include.

screens.title: A library you cannot read
screens.prose: A vendor sells a fast volatility library. You receive `fastvol.h` and `libfastvol.a`, a file of compiled object code, but no `.cpp`. Your pricer and your backtest both use it.
screens.question: What does each file do in your build?

options.text: The header lets your code compile; the `.a` is joined in by the linker

options.why: It is already compiled object code. There is nothing left to compile, only to link.

options.text: The header is enough; the `.a` is optional
options.why: The header holds only declarations. Without the `.a`, the linker reports an undefined reference.
`#include` pastes text. The `.a` is machine code, so it goes to the linker instead.

hints.text: Which file holds declarations, and which holds compiled bodies?
Follow each file's arrow.
Headers feed the compiler; compiled bodies feed the linker.

feedback.correct: Declarations to the compiler, compiled code to the linker.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow each arrow on the diagram.

byKey.hdr: The header only promises the functions exist. Without the `.a`, the linker cannot find their bodies: `undefined reference`.

explain.text: A library ships declarations in a header and bodies already compiled. A `.a` is joined in at link time; a `.so` loads when the program starts. The vendor keeps the source private and saves you the compile.

ideas: A name must be declared before it is used. A declaration gives the types and ends in `;`; a definition adds the body.
A header holds declarations and defaults; each `.cpp` compiles alone, and the linker joins the object files.
One definition per program for an ordinary function: a body in a header included by two `.cpp` files is a linker error, unless it is marked `inline`.

formula.name: Separate compilation
formula.note: `g++ -std=c++17 main.cpp returns.cpp -o backtest` does all three.

summary.trap: `#pragma once` stops one file including a header twice; it does not stop two `.cpp` files each getting a body.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: `10001LL` and `10002LL` are `long long`, so the `long long` version runs, and its division drops the half.

options.text: Nothing: two functions cannot share a name
options.why: That is true in Python, where the second `def` replaces the first. C++ keeps both and chooses by type.
The `double` version runs for `100.01` and `100.02`, so the result keeps its fraction: 100.015.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each call's argument types to a version.

explain.text: `mid(10001LL, 10002LL)` matches the `long long` version: 20003 / 2 is 10001 in integer division. `mid(100.01, 100.02)` matches the `double` version and gives 100.015.

options.why: Without `()` you name the function without calling it. It converts to `true` and prints 1, not 0.04.
`void` can appear in a declaration's empty list, but not in a call.
The function takes no arguments, so passing one is a compile error.

feedback.correct: Empty brackets call a function with no parameters.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A call always has brackets.

explain.text: A function with no parameters is still called with `()`. Without them you refer to the function itself rather than its result.

quiz.prose:
```text
$ g++ -std=c++17 main.cpp -o backtest
/usr/bin/ld: /tmp/ccR5tWb1.o: in function `main':
main.cpp:(.text+0x1a): undefined reference to `annualise(double, int)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
```
quiz.question: What is wrong?

options.text: `returns.cpp` is missing from the command, so no body was linked

options.why: Then the compiler would have stopped with `not declared`. This message comes from `ld`, the linker, after compiling worked.
A misspelt call would fail to compile. The linker is looking for the correctly spelt function and finds no body.
The message names `annualise(double, int)`, so the call compiled with both types known.

feedback.correct: Declared, called, never defined in the build.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which program printed the message?

explain.text: `ld` is the linker. `main.o` calls `annualise`, but no object file in this build defines it. Add `returns.cpp` to the command.

quiz.prose: `simple_returns` from this lesson is called with one close: `simple_returns({101.5})`.
quiz.question: How many returns does it give back?

feedback.correct: No day before it, so no return.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A return needs two closes.

byKey.one: A return compares two closes. With one close there is no yesterday, so the list is empty.

explain.text: n closes give n − 1 returns, so one close gives none. The loop from index 1 never runs.
